電子琴主體採用木製外殼與面板，多為中密度纖維板或實木製造。鍵盤由象牙塑膠或合成樹: The main body of an electric organ is a wooden case and panel, mostly of medium-density fibreboard or solid wood. The keyboard is of ivory plastic or synthetic resin, for feel and durability. Inside are circuit boards, transformers, capacitors and other electronic components, along with the speaker and amplifier. Metal is used for the stand, springs, contacts and other mechanical parts. Some higher models are covered in leather or velvet, for looks and to keep out dust. The whole design balances durability with sound.
電子琴屬電鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 52，來源地區為日本／: The electric organ is an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 52, with Japan / USA given as its region. It is played with the hands on the manuals and the feet on the volume pedal and pedalboard; a beginner can first get used to the power supply, the manuals, the pedalboard and the drawbars, then practise changing the level with the volume pedal and mixing timbres with combinations of drawbars. An instrument of this kind asks more of the player than a reed organ, since hands, feet and timbre are controlled at once, so the order is to master the sound and the pedals first and then the coordination of several manuals.
電子琴屬電鳴樂器，編號52。其音色可由音輪、簧片或電路產生不同頻率訊號，經擴大機: The electric organ is an electrophone, number 52. Its timbre can be made by tone wheels, reeds or circuits producing signals at different frequencies, sounded through an amplifier and speakers; the Hammond type can mix harmonics with drawbars to produce more than two hundred and fifty million timbres. The source gives no specific range, but mentions a second manual and a pedalboard making a three-manual layout. The volume is controlled by a single expression pedal, which sets the dynamic range, unlike a reed organ, where the bellows must be pumped.
電子琴源自簧風琴、管風琴與劇院風琴，最初模仿其音色。1897年Thaddeus: The electric organ comes from the reed organ, the pipe organ and the theatre organ, whose sounds it first imitated. In 1897 Thaddeus Cahill's Telharmonium sent music over the telephone system in New York, demonstrating the synthesis of musical tone from pure electrical waveforms; the technology was later used by Laurens Hammond in the design of his instruments. In the 1930s Hammond brought out the tonewheel organ, which makes its signal with rotating magnetic wheels instead of reeds and bellows, and added a second manual, pedals and stops; it quickly entered jazz, gospel, pop and rock. In 1934 Frederick Albert Hoschke developed the Orgatron from Benjamin Miessner's patent, blowing free reeds with a fan and amplifying them with a capacitive pickup; in 1955 Hohner brought out the Hohnerola and the Minetta. In Japan there was also Sei-ichi Yamashita's Magna Organ. After the 1970s, portable electronic organs imitating the Hammond gradually replaced the original tonewheel design.

The electric organ is an electrophonic keyboard instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 52, developed in Japan and the United States. It comes from the organ, the pipe organ and the theatre organ, whose sounds and those of the orchestra it first imitated electronically, and later it divided into the Hammond type, digital church organs, combination organs, home organs and software organs. The player uses both hands on the manuals, the feet on the pedals and the volume pedal, and drawbars to mix different frequencies and overtones. The Hammond type is common in pop, rock, country, blues, gospel and jazz; digital church organs are used mainly in church.
電子琴的聆聽場合依類型而異：哈蒙德式電子琴常見於流行、搖滾、鄉村、藍調、福音與爵: The listening occasions for the electric organ vary with the type: the Hammond organ is common in pop, rock, country, blues, gospel and jazz, and has also appeared in the line-ups of bands such as Deep Purple; digital church organs are used mainly in church, imitating the sound of the pipe organ; and there are also combination, home and software organs, played through speakers.
